children: A number of stocks jumped in the afternoon session after investors shifted toward safer consumer staples after last week’s sell-off, favoring beer, food, household, and beauty names tied to everyday spending.

A sharp drop in oil on hopes of U.S.-Iran talks eased some of the inflation strain on the market, and these steadier names rose with that turn. The main indexes opened higher, with technology and AI-related stocks firming after crude dropped on growing hopes of a U.S.-Iran deal, Reuters reported.

Bloomberg said stocks and bonds rose together after Iran’s supreme leader gave the government approval to pursue talks that could ease the war’s strain on Middle East supply. Brent sank to around $106 a barrel. Early in the session the S&P 500 was up 0.5% and the Nasdaq 100 up 0.6%, with beaten-down technology megacaps leading. West Texas Intermediate was down 6.4% at $97.48, and the 10-year yield was down four basis points at 4.89%. The shift in the tape is cheaper oil and a steadier AI trade. The beer, food, and household names above are higher alongside that rebound.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

children: Flowers Foods’s shares are somewhat volatile and have had 12 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The biggest move we wrote about over the last year was 5 months ago when the stock dropped 4.9% on the news that the Federal Reserve held rates at 3.5%–3.75% and signaled through its dot plot that the late-2025 easing cycle that had briefly offered cost relief to the sector might reverse. Fresh food distributors and producers operate on thin margins across cold-chain logistics: refrigerated transport, temperature-controlled warehousing, and just-in-time delivery networks that are energy-intensive, labor-intensive, and capital-intensive.

The Fed's revised projections confirmed that the inflation keeping all three of those cost categories elevated is not yet under control. Unlike packaged food manufacturers who can manage across inventory cycles, perishable operators face cost pressures in real time with limited ability to hedge.On the demand side, when consumers are squeezed by persistent inflation and the prospect of higher borrowing costs, they trade down from premium fresh toward frozen and packaged alternatives, compressing both volume and per-unit economics for the fresh category.

Flowers Foods is down 38.4% since the beginning of the year, and at $6.65 per share, it is trading 45.1% below its 52-week high of $12.10 from November 2025. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Flowers Foods’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at only $264.11.
